expectedText:
JOINT EMPLOYER STATUS IN STAFFING, FRANCHISE, AND PAYROLL ARRANGEMENTS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS JOINT EMPLOYER INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jordan T. Reyes, sets out what California law says about when more than one business can be the employer of the same worker at the same time — the question that arises when a worker is supplied by a staffing agency or other labor contractor, works at a franchised location, or is paid through an outside payroll company. The arrangement Acme, Inc. has described, involving Bayline Staffing Services, LLC, is: Bayline supplies approximately 30 warehouse workers who work at our Oakland facility under our shift schedules. The sheet draws on the definitions of “employ,” “employee” and “employer” in the Industrial Welfare Commission’s wage orders and on Labor Code section 18; on Martinez v. Combs (2010) 49 Cal.4th 35, which identifies the three alternative wage-order definitions of “to employ”; on Patterson v. Domino’s Pizza, LLC (2014) 60 Cal.4th 474, which addresses when a franchisor stands in an employment or agency relationship with the franchisee’s employees; on Curry v. Equilon Enterprises, LLC (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 289, which addresses whether the “ABC” test applies to joint employment; on Futrell v. Payday California, Inc. (2010) 190 Cal.App.4th 1419 and Goonewardene v. ADP, LLC (2019) 6 Cal.5th 817, which address payroll service providers; on Labor Code section 2810.3, whose separate statutory scheme is the subject of its own information sheet in this corpus; and on Government Code section 12926, subdivision (d) and Raines v. U.S. Healthworks Medical Group (2023) 15 Cal.5th 268, which address the Fair Employment and Housing Act’s inclusion of an employer’s agents within the term “employer.” This sheet reports what those sources say. It does not determine whether any particular business is or is not the employer of any particular worker, does not address federal joint-employer standards under the Fair Labor Standards Act or the National Labor Relations Act, and does not restate the independent-contractor classification rules covered elsewhere in this corpus.

WHERE THE QUESTION STARTS: THE WAGE ORDERS’ DEFINITIONS OF “EMPLOY,” “EMPLOYEE,” AND “EMPLOYER”
For claims under the Labor Code wage statutes and the Industrial Welfare Commission’s wage orders, the question whether a business is a worker’s employer begins with the wage orders’ own definitions rather than with any general-purpose definition of employment. Section 2 of each order defines the terms. In Wage Order No. 4-2001, which covers professional, technical, clerical, mechanical and similar occupations, subdivision (E) provides that “‘Employ’ means to engage, suffer, or permit to work,” and subdivision (F) provides that “‘Employee’ means any person employed by an employer.” The definition of “employer” is the one that reaches beyond a single business: subdivision (H) provides that “‘Employer’ means any person as defined in Section 18 of the Labor Code, who directly or indirectly, or through an agent or any other person, employs or exercises control over the wages, hours, or working conditions of any person.” The cross-referenced Labor Code section 18 in turn provides that “‘Person’ means any person, association, organization, partnership, business trust, limited liability company, or corporation.” The words “directly or indirectly, or through an agent or any other person” and the disjunctive “employs or exercises control” are the textual features that make it possible for the definition to describe more than one entity in a single work arrangement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "“Employ” means to engage, suffer, or permit to work."
  — Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 2(E) (IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, as printed by the Department of Industrial Relations), IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 2(E), definition of “Employ” (https://www.dir.ca.gov/iwc/IWCArticle4.pdf)
  "“Employee” means any person employed by an employer."
  — Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 2(F) (IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, as printed by the Department of Industrial Relations), IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 2(F), definition of “Employee” (https://www.dir.ca.gov/iwc/IWCArticle4.pdf)
  "“Employer” means any person as defined in Section 18 of the Labor Code, who directly or indirectly, or through an agent or any other person, employs or exercises control over the wages, hours, or working conditions of any person."
  — Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 2(H) (IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, as printed by the Department of Industrial Relations), IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 2(H), definition of “Employer” (https://www.dir.ca.gov/iwc/IWCArticle4.pdf)
  "“Person” means any person, association, organization, partnership, business trust, limited liability company, or corporation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 18 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition of “person” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=18.)
  Known gap: The quoted definitions are those of Wage Order No. 4-2001 as printed by the Department of Industrial Relations. The Industrial Welfare Commission has adopted seventeen separate wage orders, each covering different industries or occupations, and the applicable order depends on the industry or occupation at issue; the definitions of “employ,” “employee” and “employer” are worded the same way across the general industry and occupation orders, but the order that governs a given worker, and the section letters used in it, must be identified from the order itself. The wage order does not use the phrase “joint employer,” does not say how control is to be measured, and does not state what quantum of control makes a second business an employer; those questions are addressed by case law. Two printings of the order published by the Department of Industrial Relations were compared for this clause — the current printing (IWC Form 1104, Rev. 11/2018) and the Department’s 2006 printing of the same order — and the quoted definitions are identical in both; the two printings render the typographic quotation marks around the defined terms differently in their extracted text layers, and the quotations here use typographic quotation marks. Nothing in this clause states the definitions used for other purposes, such as workers’ compensation, unemployment insurance, or tax law, which are defined by their own statutes.

MARTINEZ V. COMBS: “TO EMPLOY” HAS THREE ALTERNATIVE DEFINITIONS
In Martinez v. Combs (2010) 49 Cal.4th 35, farmworkers who had been employed by a strawberry grower sought unpaid wages from produce merchants who bought the grower’s crop, on the theory that the merchants were also their employers. The California Supreme Court held that the wage order’s definitions govern that question in an action under Labor Code section 1194, and it read those definitions as stating three separate ways an entity can be an employer. The court wrote: “To employ, then, under the IWC’s definition, has three alternative definitions. It means: (a) to exercise control over the wages, hours or working conditions, or (b) to suffer or permit to work, or (c) to engage, thereby creating a common law employment relationship.” Because the definitions are alternatives, a business can be an employer by satisfying any one of them; the common law employment relationship described in the third alternative is one route to employer status under the wage order, not the only one. Applying that framework, the court concluded on the record before it that the merchants were not the workers’ employers, while also noting that the “employer” definition “is broad enough to reach through straw men and other sham arrangements to impose liability for wages on the actual employer.”

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "To employ, then, under the IWC’s definition, has three alternative definitions. It means: (a) to exercise control over the wages, hours or working conditions, or (b) to suffer or permit to work, or (c) to engage, thereby creating a common law employment relationship."
  — Martinez v. Combs, (2010) 49 Cal.4th 35 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2630272/martinez-v-combs/)
  "is broad enough to reach through straw men and other sham arrangements to impose liability for wages on the actual employer."
  — Martinez v. Combs, (2010) 49 Cal.4th 35 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2630272/martinez-v-combs/)
  Known gap: The three-part formulation appears in a decision construing the wage orders in an action for unpaid minimum wages under Labor Code section 1194; Martinez does not hold that the same definitions govern every California statute that uses the word “employer,” and other statutes carry their own definitions. Martinez does not state a threshold or checklist for how much control over wages, hours, or working conditions is enough, and it decided the merchants’ status on the undisputed facts of that record rather than announcing a general rule about produce buyers or about any other category of business. The “straw men” sentence is quoted here beginning with the words “is broad enough” because the reporter text places a footnote-reference marker between the preceding quoted wage-order language and those words; the subject of that sentence, supplied in the body above, is the wage order’s definition of “employer.” The source consulted is the CourtListener reporter text of the opinion, whose optical-character-recognition layer contains occasional artifacts elsewhere in the opinion; each sentence quoted here was separately confirmed through CourtListener’s public search index as a phrase occurring in this opinion.

THE WAGE ORDER DEFINITION CONTEMPLATES MORE THAN ONE EMPLOYER, AND DOES NOT IMPORT THE FEDERAL TEST
Martinez explained why the wage order’s definition of “employer” is capable of describing several businesses at once. The court stated that “the wage orders’ language mirrors the scope of the IWC’s regulatory authority over wages, hours and working conditions (§ 1173) and by its terms imposes liability on multiple entities who divide among themselves control over those different aspects of the employment relationship.” The court also declined an invitation to read the federal “economic reality” test developed under the Fair Labor Standards Act into the wage orders, stating: “We see no reason to substitute this definition of employment, which has no basis in California law, for definitions in wage orders regularly adopted by the IWC.” It observed that although the Industrial Welfare Commission has at times deliberately incorporated federal law into particular wage order provisions, “No wage order, however, incorporates federal law in defining the terms ‘employ’ or ‘employer.’”

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "the wage orders’ language mirrors the scope of the IWC’s regulatory authority over wages, hours and working conditions (§ 1173) and by its terms imposes liability on multiple entities who divide among themselves control over those different aspects of the employment relationship."
  — Martinez v. Combs, (2010) 49 Cal.4th 35 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2630272/martinez-v-combs/)
  "We see no reason to substitute this definition of employment, which has no basis in California law, for definitions in wage orders regularly adopted by the IWC."
  — Martinez v. Combs, (2010) 49 Cal.4th 35 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2630272/martinez-v-combs/)
  "No wage order, however, incorporates federal law in defining the terms “employ” or “employer.”"
  — Martinez v. Combs, (2010) 49 Cal.4th 35 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2630272/martinez-v-combs/)
  Known gap: These statements describe the wage orders and the Labor Code wage statutes. They do not describe the tests used under federal statutes, which have their own standards and their own agency regulations, and Martinez does not decide how a federal joint-employer question would come out on the same facts. The sentence about liability on “multiple entities” states that the definition is capable of reaching more than one business; it does not say that any particular division of control between two businesses makes both of them employers, and Martinez supplies no formula for allocating control. The source consulted is the CourtListener reporter text of the opinion; each sentence quoted here was separately confirmed through CourtListener’s public search index as a phrase occurring in this opinion.

WHAT “SUFFER OR PERMIT TO WORK” MEANS, AND WHY BENEFITING FROM THE WORK IS NOT ENOUGH
The second of the three Martinez alternatives — to “suffer or permit to work” — has a historical meaning that the court traced to child-labor statutes and declined to depart from. The court described its present-day operation this way: “A proprietor who knows that persons are working in his or her business without having been formally hired, or while being paid less than the minimum wage, clearly suffers or permits that work by failing to prevent it, while having the power to do so.” The plaintiffs in Martinez argued that the merchants suffered or permitted their work because the merchants knew the work was occurring and benefited from it. The court rejected benefit as the measure, stating: “However, the concept of a benefit is neither a necessary nor a sufficient condition for liability under the ‘suffer or permit’ standard.” A Court of Appeal later applied that reading in a case about a fuel company and the workers of its independent station operator, describing suffering as concerning “the alleged employer’s failure to hinder the alleged employee’s work by not stopping the alleged employee from working.”

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "A proprietor who knows that persons are working in his or her business without having been formally hired, or while being paid less than the minimum wage, clearly suffers or permits that work by failing to prevent it, while having the power to do so."
  — Martinez v. Combs, (2010) 49 Cal.4th 35 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2630272/martinez-v-combs/)
  "However, the concept of a benefit is neither a necessary nor a sufficient condition for liability under the “suffer or permit” standard."
  — Martinez v. Combs, (2010) 49 Cal.4th 35 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2630272/martinez-v-combs/)
  "Suffering concerns the alleged employer’s failure to hinder the alleged employee’s work by not stopping the alleged employee from working"
  — Curry v. Equilon Enterprises, LLC, (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 289 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4499379/curry-v-equilon-enterprises-llc/)
  Known gap: The quoted description of what it means to suffer or permit work is framed in terms of knowledge of the work together with the power to prevent it; Martinez does not state what facts establish that power in any particular arrangement, and the opinion resolved the merchants’ status on the undisputed facts of that record. The final quotation is drawn from Curry v. Equilon Enterprises, LLC (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 289, a decision of the Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District; it describes how that court read Martinez and is not a holding of the California Supreme Court. The sources consulted are the CourtListener texts of the two opinions; the Martinez sentences were separately confirmed through CourtListener’s public search index, and the Curry sentence was verified against two separate CourtListener records of the same opinion; the second of those records inserts a star-pagination marker (“*312”) in the middle of the quoted sentence, and the quotation above follows the record that does not.

FRANCHISE ARRANGEMENTS: PATTERSON V. DOMINO’S PIZZA AND THE GENERAL RIGHT OF CONTROL
Patterson v. Domino’s Pizza, LLC (2014) 60 Cal.4th 474 addressed whether a franchisor stands in an employment or agency relationship with a franchisee and its employees, in a case brought by an employee of a franchised pizza store who alleged sexual harassment by the franchisee’s supervisor. The court began from the structure of the franchise relationship, observing that “It is the franchisee who implements the operational standards on a day-to-day basis, hires and fires store employees, and regulates workplace behavior.” It held that brand-wide operating standards alone do not convert a franchisor into the employer of the franchisee’s workers: “The imposition and enforcement of a uniform marketing and operational plan cannot automatically saddle the franchisor with responsibility for employees of the franchisee who injure each other on the job.” The standard the court stated is one of retained or assumed general control: “It follows that potential liability on the theories pled here requires that the franchisor exhibit the traditionally understood characteristics of an ‘employer’ or ‘principal’; i.e., it has retained or assumed a general right of control over factors such as hiring, direction, supervision, discipline, discharge, and relevant day-to-day aspects of the workplace behavior of the franchisee’s employees.” The court added that the result is not a categorical immunity: “A franchisor will be liable if it has retained or assumed the right of general control over the relevant day-to-day operations at its franchised locations that we have described, and cannot escape liability in such a case merely because it failed or declined to establish a policy with regard to that particular conduct.”

  — Patterson v. Domino’s Pizza, LLC, (2014) 60 Cal.4th 474 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2721744/patterson-v-dominos-pizza-llc/)

  Known gap: Patterson arose on summary judgment in a case pleading claims under the Fair Employment and Housing Act and related tort theories against a franchisor, and the court stated that its holding “is limited to determining the circumstances under which an employment or agency relationship exists as a prerequisite to pursuing statutory and tort theories like those alleged against the franchisor here.” The opinion states that applying the FEHA test for an employment relationship “produces no different result in this franchising case than the one we have already reached,” but it does not decide how the separate wage-order definitions discussed elsewhere in this sheet apply to a franchise arrangement, and it does not address Labor Code section 2810.3, which was enacted the year after Patterson was decided. Whether a given franchisor has retained or assumed the described general right of control is a fact question that Patterson resolved on the record before it. The source consulted is the CourtListener reporter text of the opinion, fetched twice with distinct request headers; the quoted sentence about the uniform marketing and operational plan was separately confirmed through CourtListener’s public search index as a phrase occurring in this opinion.

JOINT EMPLOYMENT IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION FROM INDEPENDENT-CONTRACTOR MISCLASSIFICATION
The “ABC” test announced in Dynamex Operations West, Inc. v. Superior Court (2018) 4 Cal.5th 903 and later codified in the Labor Code addresses whether a worker has been misclassified as an independent contractor rather than an employee. Curry v. Equilon Enterprises, LLC (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 289 addressed whether that test also governs the different question of whether a second business is an employer of someone who is already someone else’s employee. The court described the difference: “In the joint employment context, the alleged employee is already considered an employee of the primary employer; the issue is whether the employee is also an employee of the alleged secondary employer.” Because the policy reasons the Supreme Court gave for placing the burden on the hiring entity under the ABC test concerned misclassified independent contractors — unpaid taxes and the absence of employment-law protections — the Court of Appeal reasoned that those reasons are “not relevant in the joint employment context” and concluded: “Therefore, it does not appear that the Supreme Court intended for the ‘ABC’ test to be applied in joint employment cases.” The court instead applied the Martinez definitions to the joint-employment question before it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "In the joint employment context, the alleged employee is already considered an employee of the primary employer; the issue is whether the employee is also an employee of the alleged secondary employer."
  — Curry v. Equilon Enterprises, LLC, (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 289 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4499379/curry-v-equilon-enterprises-llc/)
  "Therefore, it does not appear that the Supreme Court intended for the “ABC” test to be applied in joint employment cases."
  — Curry v. Equilon Enterprises, LLC, (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 289 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4499379/curry-v-equilon-enterprises-llc/)
  Known gap: Curry is a decision of the Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division Two; it is not a decision of the California Supreme Court, and this clause does not survey later Court of Appeal decisions that have agreed or disagreed with its reasoning, nor any subsequent statutory changes to the classification statutes. The quoted conclusion is phrased by the court itself in terms of what the Supreme Court appears to have intended rather than as a categorical rule. This clause states only which test Curry applied to the joint-employment question; it does not state how the ABC test itself operates, which is the subject of a separate information sheet in this corpus, and it does not state the outcome for any particular arrangement. The opinion was verified against two separate CourtListener records of the same decision, and the quoted conclusion was separately confirmed through CourtListener’s public search index.

OUTSIDE PAYROLL COMPANIES: HANDLING THE PAYROLL IS NOT THE SAME AS CONTROLLING WAGES
A business that issues the paychecks is not for that reason the employer under the wage statutes. In Futrell v. Payday California, Inc. (2010) 190 Cal.App.4th 1419, a worker on a commercial production sued the payroll company that calculated his pay and issued his checks from its own bank account. The Court of Appeal said it would “apply the Martinez definition” in “cases involving the issue of whether an employer-employee relationship existed for purposes of the Labor Code wage statutes,” and it then construed the first Martinez alternative: “we conclude that ‘control over wages’ means that a person or entity has the power or authority to negotiate and set an employee’s rate of pay, and not that a person or entity is physically involved in the preparation of an employee’s paycheck.” It added: “The task of preparing payroll, whether done by an internal division or department of an employer, or by an outside vendor of an employer, does not make Payday an employer for purposes of liability for wages under the Labor Code wage statutes.” The California Supreme Court recounted that line of authority in Goonewardene v. ADP, LLC (2019) 6 Cal.5th 817, describing the Court of Appeal in that case as “agreeing with prior appellate court decisions that a payroll company cannot properly be considered an employer of the hiring business’s employee that may be liable under the applicable labor statutes for failure to pay wages that are due.”

  "we conclude that “control over wages” means that a person or entity has the power or authority to negotiate and set an employee’s rate of pay, and not that a person or entity is physically involved in the preparation of an employee’s paycheck."
  — Futrell v. Payday California, Inc., (2010) 190 Cal.App.4th 1419 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5809907/futrell-v-payday-california-inc/)

  — Futrell v. Payday California, Inc., (2010) 190 Cal.App.4th 1419 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5809907/futrell-v-payday-california-inc/)

  Known gap: Futrell is a decision of the Court of Appeal, Second Appellate District. The quoted sentence from Goonewardene appears in the Supreme Court’s statement of the case, describing the Court of Appeal’s ruling below; the issues the Supreme Court granted review to decide in Goonewardene were whether an employee may sue a payroll company on third party beneficiary, negligence and negligent misrepresentation theories, not whether a payroll company is an employer, so the quoted words report the lower court’s conclusion rather than an independent holding of the Supreme Court on that point. Neither decision addresses a payroll or staffing company that also negotiates or sets pay rates, hires, fires, or supervises, and Futrell’s reading of “control over wages” addresses only the first of the three Martinez alternatives. The sources consulted are the CourtListener texts of the two opinions, each fetched twice with distinct request headers, and the quoted sentences were separately confirmed through CourtListener’s public search index.

LABOR CODE SECTION 2810.3 IS A SEPARATE, ADDITIONAL SCHEME — NOT A REPLACEMENT FOR THE COMMON-LAW ANALYSIS
Alongside the wage-order and case-law analysis, the Legislature has enacted a statute that allocates specified liability between a business that obtains workers through a labor contractor and that contractor. Labor Code section 2810.3 provides that “A client employer shall share with a labor contractor all civil legal responsibility and civil liability for all workers supplied by that labor contractor” for the payment of wages and for the failure to secure valid workers’ compensation coverage. That statute has its own coverage limits: among the entities excluded from the definition of “client employer” is “A business entity with a workforce of fewer than 25 workers, including those hired directly by the client employer and those obtained from, or provided by, any labor contractor.” The statute states that it does not displace other sources of liability: “The provisions of subdivisions (b) and (c) are in addition to, and shall be supplemental of, any other theories of liability or requirement established by statute or common law.” That sentence is what keeps the wage-order and case-law joint-employment analysis in place alongside the statute, and it also means that falling outside section 2810.3’s coverage thresholds does not by itself answer the separate question of who is an employer under the wage orders.

UNDER FEHA, “EMPLOYER” INCLUDES AN EMPLOYER’S AGENT, INCLUDING A BUSINESS HIRED TO SCREEN APPLICANTS
The Fair Employment and Housing Act reaches a second business by a different route: its definition of “employer” expressly includes agents. Government Code section 12926, subdivision (d) provides that “‘Employer’ includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities, except as follows:”, followed by an exception for a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit. In Raines v. U.S. Healthworks Medical Group (2023) 15 Cal.5th 268, answering a question certified by the Ninth Circuit in a case about pre-employment medical screenings performed by an outside provider for prospective employers, the California Supreme Court read that agent language as creating direct liability for the agent. Its conclusion states that FEHA “permits a business entity acting as an agent of an employer to be held directly liable as an employer for employment discrimination in violation of the FEHA in appropriate circumstances when the business-entity agent has at least five employees and carries out FEHA-regulated activities on behalf of an employer.”

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "“Employer” includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities, except as follows:"
  — Cal. Government Code § 12926(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, FEHA definition of “employer” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12926.)
  "permits a business entity acting as an agent of an employer to be held directly liable as an employer for employment discrimination in violation of the FEHA in appropriate circumstances when the business-entity agent has at least five employees and carries out FEHA-regulated activities on behalf of an employer."
  — Raines v. U.S. Healthworks Medical Group, (2023) 15 Cal.5th 268 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9421500/raines-v-us-healthworks-medical-group/)

  — Raines v. U.S. Healthworks Medical Group, (2023) 15 Cal.5th 268 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9421500/raines-v-us-healthworks-medical-group/)

expectedJSON.body: This information sheet, prepared by Jordan T. Reyes, sets out what California law says about when more than one business can be the employer of the same worker at the same time — the question that arises when a worker is supplied by a staffing agency or other labor contractor, works at a franchised location, or is paid through an outside payroll company. The arrangement Acme, Inc. has described, involving Bayline Staffing Services, LLC, is: Bayline supplies approximately 30 warehouse workers who work at our Oakland facility under our shift schedules. The sheet draws on the definitions of “employ,” “employee” and “employer” in the Industrial Welfare Commission’s wage orders and on Labor Code section 18; on Martinez v. Combs (2010) 49 Cal.4th 35, which identifies the three alternative wage-order definitions of “to employ”; on Patterson v. Domino’s Pizza, LLC (2014) 60 Cal.4th 474, which addresses when a franchisor stands in an employment or agency relationship with the franchisee’s employees; on Curry v. Equilon Enterprises, LLC (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 289, which addresses whether the “ABC” test applies to joint employment; on Futrell v. Payday California, Inc. (2010) 190 Cal.App.4th 1419 and Goonewardene v. ADP, LLC (2019) 6 Cal.5th 817, which address payroll service providers; on Labor Code section 2810.3, whose separate statutory scheme is the subject of its own information sheet in this corpus; and on Government Code section 12926, subdivision (d) and Raines v. U.S. Healthworks Medical Group (2023) 15 Cal.5th 268, which address the Fair Employment and Housing Act’s inclusion of an employer’s agents within the term “employer.” This sheet reports what those sources say. It does not determine whether any particular business is or is not the employer of any particular worker, does not address federal joint-employer standards under the Fair Labor Standards Act or the National Labor Relations Act, and does not restate the independent-contractor classification rules covered elsewhere in this corpus.

For claims under the Labor Code wage statutes and the Industrial Welfare Commission’s wage orders, the question whether a business is a worker’s employer begins with the wage orders’ own definitions rather than with any general-purpose definition of employment. Section 2 of each order defines the terms. In Wage Order No. 4-2001, which covers professional, technical, clerical, mechanical and similar occupations, subdivision (E) provides that “‘Employ’ means to engage, suffer, or permit to work,” and subdivision (F) provides that “‘Employee’ means any person employed by an employer.” The definition of “employer” is the one that reaches beyond a single business: subdivision (H) provides that “‘Employer’ means any person as defined in Section 18 of the Labor Code, who directly or indirectly, or through an agent or any other person, employs or exercises control over the wages, hours, or working conditions of any person.” The cross-referenced Labor Code section 18 in turn provides that “‘Person’ means any person, association, organization, partnership, business trust, limited liability company, or corporation.” The words “directly or indirectly, or through an agent or any other person” and the disjunctive “employs or exercises control” are the textual features that make it possible for the definition to describe more than one entity in a single work arrangement.

expectedJSON.gap: The quoted definitions are those of Wage Order No. 4-2001 as printed by the Department of Industrial Relations. The Industrial Welfare Commission has adopted seventeen separate wage orders, each covering different industries or occupations, and the applicable order depends on the industry or occupation at issue; the definitions of “employ,” “employee” and “employer” are worded the same way across the general industry and occupation orders, but the order that governs a given worker, and the section letters used in it, must be identified from the order itself. The wage order does not use the phrase “joint employer,” does not say how control is to be measured, and does not state what quantum of control makes a second business an employer; those questions are addressed by case law. Two printings of the order published by the Department of Industrial Relations were compared for this clause — the current printing (IWC Form 1104, Rev. 11/2018) and the Department’s 2006 printing of the same order — and the quoted definitions are identical in both; the two printings render the typographic quotation marks around the defined terms differently in their extracted text layers, and the quotations here use typographic quotation marks. Nothing in this clause states the definitions used for other purposes, such as workers’ compensation, unemployment insurance, or tax law, which are defined by their own statutes.

expectedJSON.body: In Martinez v. Combs (2010) 49 Cal.4th 35, farmworkers who had been employed by a strawberry grower sought unpaid wages from produce merchants who bought the grower’s crop, on the theory that the merchants were also their employers. The California Supreme Court held that the wage order’s definitions govern that question in an action under Labor Code section 1194, and it read those definitions as stating three separate ways an entity can be an employer. The court wrote: “To employ, then, under the IWC’s definition, has three alternative definitions. It means: (a) to exercise control over the wages, hours or working conditions, or (b) to suffer or permit to work, or (c) to engage, thereby creating a common law employment relationship.” Because the definitions are alternatives, a business can be an employer by satisfying any one of them; the common law employment relationship described in the third alternative is one route to employer status under the wage order, not the only one. Applying that framework, the court concluded on the record before it that the merchants were not the workers’ employers, while also noting that the “employer” definition “is broad enough to reach through straw men and other sham arrangements to impose liability for wages on the actual employer.”

citations.quote: To employ, then, under the IWC’s definition, has three alternative definitions. It means: (a) to exercise control over the wages, hours or working conditions, or (b) to suffer or permit to work, or (c) to engage, thereby creating a common law employment relationship.
is broad enough to reach through straw men and other sham arrangements to impose liability for wages on the actual employer.

expectedJSON.gap: The three-part formulation appears in a decision construing the wage orders in an action for unpaid minimum wages under Labor Code section 1194; Martinez does not hold that the same definitions govern every California statute that uses the word “employer,” and other statutes carry their own definitions. Martinez does not state a threshold or checklist for how much control over wages, hours, or working conditions is enough, and it decided the merchants’ status on the undisputed facts of that record rather than announcing a general rule about produce buyers or about any other category of business. The “straw men” sentence is quoted here beginning with the words “is broad enough” because the reporter text places a footnote-reference marker between the preceding quoted wage-order language and those words; the subject of that sentence, supplied in the body above, is the wage order’s definition of “employer.” The source consulted is the CourtListener reporter text of the opinion, whose optical-character-recognition layer contains occasional artifacts elsewhere in the opinion; each sentence quoted here was separately confirmed through CourtListener’s public search index as a phrase occurring in this opinion.

expectedJSON.body: Martinez explained why the wage order’s definition of “employer” is capable of describing several businesses at once. The court stated that “the wage orders’ language mirrors the scope of the IWC’s regulatory authority over wages, hours and working conditions (§ 1173) and by its terms imposes liability on multiple entities who divide among themselves control over those different aspects of the employment relationship.” The court also declined an invitation to read the federal “economic reality” test developed under the Fair Labor Standards Act into the wage orders, stating: “We see no reason to substitute this definition of employment, which has no basis in California law, for definitions in wage orders regularly adopted by the IWC.” It observed that although the Industrial Welfare Commission has at times deliberately incorporated federal law into particular wage order provisions, “No wage order, however, incorporates federal law in defining the terms ‘employ’ or ‘employer.’”

We see no reason to substitute this definition of employment, which has no basis in California law, for definitions in wage orders regularly adopted by the IWC.

expectedJSON.gap: These statements describe the wage orders and the Labor Code wage statutes. They do not describe the tests used under federal statutes, which have their own standards and their own agency regulations, and Martinez does not decide how a federal joint-employer question would come out on the same facts. The sentence about liability on “multiple entities” states that the definition is capable of reaching more than one business; it does not say that any particular division of control between two businesses makes both of them employers, and Martinez supplies no formula for allocating control. The source consulted is the CourtListener reporter text of the opinion; each sentence quoted here was separately confirmed through CourtListener’s public search index as a phrase occurring in this opinion.

expectedJSON.body: The second of the three Martinez alternatives — to “suffer or permit to work” — has a historical meaning that the court traced to child-labor statutes and declined to depart from. The court described its present-day operation this way: “A proprietor who knows that persons are working in his or her business without having been formally hired, or while being paid less than the minimum wage, clearly suffers or permits that work by failing to prevent it, while having the power to do so.” The plaintiffs in Martinez argued that the merchants suffered or permitted their work because the merchants knew the work was occurring and benefited from it. The court rejected benefit as the measure, stating: “However, the concept of a benefit is neither a necessary nor a sufficient condition for liability under the ‘suffer or permit’ standard.” A Court of Appeal later applied that reading in a case about a fuel company and the workers of its independent station operator, describing suffering as concerning “the alleged employer’s failure to hinder the alleged employee’s work by not stopping the alleged employee from working.”

citations.quote: A proprietor who knows that persons are working in his or her business without having been formally hired, or while being paid less than the minimum wage, clearly suffers or permits that work by failing to prevent it, while having the power to do so.
However, the concept of a benefit is neither a necessary nor a sufficient condition for liability under the “suffer or permit” standard.
Suffering concerns the alleged employer’s failure to hinder the alleged employee’s work by not stopping the alleged employee from working

The final quotation is drawn from Curry v. Equilon Enterprises, LLC (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 289, a decision of the Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District; it describes how that court read Martinez and is not a holding of the California Supreme Court. expectedJSON.body: Patterson v. Domino’s Pizza, LLC (2014) 60 Cal.4th 474 addressed whether a franchisor stands in an employment or agency relationship with a franchisee and its employees, in a case brought by an employee of a franchised pizza store who alleged sexual harassment by the franchisee’s supervisor. The court began from the structure of the franchise relationship, observing that “It is the franchisee who implements the operational standards on a day-to-day basis, hires and fires store employees, and regulates workplace behavior.” It held that brand-wide operating standards alone do not convert a franchisor into the employer of the franchisee’s workers: “The imposition and enforcement of a uniform marketing and operational plan cannot automatically saddle the franchisor with responsibility for employees of the franchisee who injure each other on the job.” The standard the court stated is one of retained or assumed general control: “It follows that potential liability on the theories pled here requires that the franchisor exhibit the traditionally understood characteristics of an ‘employer’ or ‘principal’; i.e., it has retained or assumed a general right of control over factors such as hiring, direction, supervision, discipline, discharge, and relevant day-to-day aspects of the workplace behavior of the franchisee’s employees.” The court added that the result is not a categorical immunity: “A franchisor will be liable if it has retained or assumed the right of general control over the relevant day-to-day operations at its franchised locations that we have described, and cannot escape liability in such a case merely because it failed or declined to establish a policy with regard to that particular conduct.”

The imposition and enforcement of a uniform marketing and operational plan cannot automatically saddle the franchisor with responsibility for employees of the franchisee who injure each other on the job.

It follows that potential liability on the theories pled here requires that the franchisor exhibit the traditionally understood characteristics of an “employer” or “principal”; i.e., it has retained or assumed a general right of control over factors such as hiring, direction, supervision, discipline, discharge, and relevant day-to-day aspects of the workplace behavior of the franchisee’s employees.

A franchisor will be liable if it has retained or assumed the right of general control over the relevant day-to-day operations at its franchised locations that we have described, and cannot escape liability in such a case merely because it failed or declined to establish a policy with regard to that particular conduct.
Application of the FEHA test for determining an employment relationship produces no different result in this franchising case than the one we have already reached.

Whether a given franchisor has retained or assumed the described general right of control is a fact question that Patterson resolved on the record before it. expectedJSON.body: The “ABC” test announced in Dynamex Operations West, Inc. v. Superior Court (2018) 4 Cal.5th 903 and later codified in the Labor Code addresses whether a worker has been misclassified as an independent contractor rather than an employee. Curry v. Equilon Enterprises, LLC (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 289 addressed whether that test also governs the different question of whether a second business is an employer of someone who is already someone else’s employee. The court described the difference: “In the joint employment context, the alleged employee is already considered an employee of the primary employer; the issue is whether the employee is also an employee of the alleged secondary employer.” Because the policy reasons the Supreme Court gave for placing the burden on the hiring entity under the ABC test concerned misclassified independent contractors — unpaid taxes and the absence of employment-law protections — the Court of Appeal reasoned that those reasons are “not relevant in the joint employment context” and concluded: “Therefore, it does not appear that the Supreme Court intended for the ‘ABC’ test to be applied in joint employment cases.” The court instead applied the Martinez definitions to the joint-employment question before it.

citations.quote: In the joint employment context, the alleged employee is already considered an employee of the primary employer; the issue is whether the employee is also an employee of the alleged secondary employer.
Therefore, it does not appear that the Supreme Court intended for the “ABC” test to be applied in joint employment cases.

expectedJSON.gap: Curry is a decision of the Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division Two; it is not a decision of the California Supreme Court, and this clause does not survey later Court of Appeal decisions that have agreed or disagreed with its reasoning, nor any subsequent statutory changes to the classification statutes. The quoted conclusion is phrased by the court itself in terms of what the Supreme Court appears to have intended rather than as a categorical rule. This clause states only which test Curry applied to the joint-employment question; it does not state how the ABC test itself operates, which is the subject of a separate information sheet in this corpus, and it does not state the outcome for any particular arrangement. The opinion was verified against two separate CourtListener records of the same decision, and the quoted conclusion was separately confirmed through CourtListener’s public search index.

expectedJSON.body: A business that issues the paychecks is not for that reason the employer under the wage statutes. In Futrell v. Payday California, Inc. (2010) 190 Cal.App.4th 1419, a worker on a commercial production sued the payroll company that calculated his pay and issued his checks from its own bank account. The Court of Appeal said it would “apply the Martinez definition” in “cases involving the issue of whether an employer-employee relationship existed for purposes of the Labor Code wage statutes,” and it then construed the first Martinez alternative: “we conclude that ‘control over wages’ means that a person or entity has the power or authority to negotiate and set an employee’s rate of pay, and not that a person or entity is physically involved in the preparation of an employee’s paycheck.” It added: “The task of preparing payroll, whether done by an internal division or department of an employer, or by an outside vendor of an employer, does not make Payday an employer for purposes of liability for wages under the Labor Code wage statutes.” The California Supreme Court recounted that line of authority in Goonewardene v. ADP, LLC (2019) 6 Cal.5th 817, describing the Court of Appeal in that case as “agreeing with prior appellate court decisions that a payroll company cannot properly be considered an employer of the hiring business’s employee that may be liable under the applicable labor statutes for failure to pay wages that are due.”

citations.quote: in cases involving the issue of whether an employer-employee relationship existed for purposes of the Labor Code wage statutes, we will apply the Martinez definition.

we conclude that “control over wages” means that a person or entity has the power or authority to negotiate and set an employee’s rate of pay, and not that a person or entity is physically involved in the preparation of an employee’s paycheck.

The task of preparing payroll, whether done by an internal division or department of an employer, or by an outside vendor of an employer, does not make Payday an employer for purposes of liability for wages under the Labor Code wage statutes.
a payroll company cannot properly be considered an employer of the hiring business’s employee that may be liable under the applicable labor statutes for failure to pay wages that are due

expectedJSON.gap: Futrell is a decision of the Court of Appeal, Second Appellate District. The quoted sentence from Goonewardene appears in the Supreme Court’s statement of the case, describing the Court of Appeal’s ruling below; the issues the Supreme Court granted review to decide in Goonewardene were whether an employee may sue a payroll company on third party beneficiary, negligence and negligent misrepresentation theories, not whether a payroll company is an employer, so the quoted words report the lower court’s conclusion rather than an independent holding of the Supreme Court on that point. Neither decision addresses a payroll or staffing company that also negotiates or sets pay rates, hires, fires, or supervises, and Futrell’s reading of “control over wages” addresses only the first of the three Martinez alternatives. The sources consulted are the CourtListener texts of the two opinions, each fetched twice with distinct request headers, and the quoted sentences were separately confirmed through CourtListener’s public search index.

expectedJSON.body: Alongside the wage-order and case-law analysis, the Legislature has enacted a statute that allocates specified liability between a business that obtains workers through a labor contractor and that contractor. Labor Code section 2810.3 provides that “A client employer shall share with a labor contractor all civil legal responsibility and civil liability for all workers supplied by that labor contractor” for the payment of wages and for the failure to secure valid workers’ compensation coverage. That statute has its own coverage limits: among the entities excluded from the definition of “client employer” is “A business entity with a workforce of fewer than 25 workers, including those hired directly by the client employer and those obtained from, or provided by, any labor contractor.” The statute states that it does not displace other sources of liability: “The provisions of subdivisions (b) and (c) are in addition to, and shall be supplemental of, any other theories of liability or requirement established by statute or common law.” That sentence is what keeps the wage-order and case-law joint-employment analysis in place alongside the statute, and it also means that falling outside section 2810.3’s coverage thresholds does not by itself answer the separate question of who is an employer under the wage orders.

expectedJSON.body: The Fair Employment and Housing Act reaches a second business by a different route: its definition of “employer” expressly includes agents. Government Code section 12926, subdivision (d) provides that “‘Employer’ includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities, except as follows:”, followed by an exception for a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit. In Raines v. U.S. Healthworks Medical Group (2023) 15 Cal.5th 268, answering a question certified by the Ninth Circuit in a case about pre-employment medical screenings performed by an outside provider for prospective employers, the California Supreme Court read that agent language as creating direct liability for the agent. Its conclusion states that FEHA “permits a business entity acting as an agent of an employer to be held directly liable as an employer for employment discrimination in violation of the FEHA in appropriate circumstances when the business-entity agent has at least five employees and carries out FEHA-regulated activities on behalf of an employer.”
